quote_item6: Videos were classified as “factual” if they corresponded to safe food handling recommendations from the CDC and Health Canada, including washing produce only with running water and not storing pre-cut or ready-to-eat produce at room temperature for >2 h (6, 16).

Item 6 HIGH: 'nonfactual' = departure from CDC/Health Canada safe-handling GUIDANCE, i.e. guideline-adherence standing in for falsity (project CONTENT-vs-QUALITY rule). Item 7 HIGH: one coder, second 'validated' the coding, no kappa/alpha. Items 4/5 NA (pure content analysis). Item 9 LOW: collection date (Oct 2021) and video date ranges stated. quote_item6: The codebook reflected public health guidance related to COVID-19 and served as a reference to identify misinformation (see Supplemental Material).

notes: Item 6 HIGH: author-devised low/moderate/high codebook benchmarked to public-health guidance and 'scientific consensus', not to fact-check verdicts or a validated list. Item 7 LOW: reliability handled (all reviewers coded first 9 videos, discrepancies adjudicated, interrater consistency >90% before independent coding) - raw agreement only, no kappa. quote_item6: A 5-point Likert scale was used to demonstrate the level of misinformation compared to American Urological Association and National Comprehensive Cancer Network guidelines.
quote_item10: On 12 August 2021, a cookie-free, cache-cleared, incognito Safari browser was used to obtain the top 50 videos for the search term ‘prostate cancer screening’ on both YT and TK.
notes: Weakest study in the shard. Item 6 HIGH: misinformation operationalised as three reviewers' agreement with 'this video does not contain misinformation' on a 5-point Likert, benchmarked to AUA/NCCN SCREENING GUIDELINES - guideline non-adherence, not falsity. Item 7 HIGH: no kappa/ICC/agreement statistic anywhere in the paper (DISCERN/PEMAT are validated but measure information quality, not the misinformation outcome). Item 3 HIGH: top-50 by platform default ranking. Item 9 HIGH: single-day extraction, and the two platform corpora span very different periods (46% of YT videos >5 years old, all TK videos <1 year). Item 10 HIGH: denominator = 50 top search results per platform.

quote_item6: To classify news domains as unreliable, we used a combination of two lists used in previous work (see Methods, ‘Unreliable news classifications’). The first is from peer-reviewed work that classified news domains as unreliable on the basis of a manual review of their editorial practices. The second was obtained from NewsGuard, an independent organization that employs journalists and editors to review and rate news domains on the basis of nine journalistic criteria.
quote_item10: In 2018, we collected exposure to 102,114 Google Search result pages for 275 participants, follows on 279,680 Google Search results for 262 participants and overall engagement with 14,677,297 URLs for 333 participants.
notes: The clear LOW of the shard, and the discriminating case for item 10. Ecologically valid browser-extension capture of every Google SERP actually rendered in participants' browsers plus their full browsing history: denominator is the real audience's entire search-exposure stream (and, for overall engagement, their entire URL stream), not a curated topical corpus. Item 6/7 LOW: peer-reviewed unreliable-domain list plus NewsGuard. Item 5 LOW: behavioural trace from the subjects themselves. Item 4 HIGH: extension install was opt-in and the authors state 'a non-random subset of these respondents opted in'; no response/attrition rates reported. Item 3 LOW on the strength of the complete behavioural trace and panel quota/matched recruitment, though recruitment was not probability sampling. Item 8 LOW within wave; note the follow measure changed between waves (Google History 2018, Tab Activity 2020) and estimates are reported per wave. Superscript reference markers stripped from the item-6 quote; wording otherwise verbatim.

quote_item6: The 25,080 topic-coded Facebook pages were coded as a fake news source if they matched a URL in the Grinberg et al. quote_item10: Among our 806 subjects, 18.36% (n = 148) liked at least one Facebook page for a fake news source, answering RQ1.
notes: Item 10 LOW despite the convenience sample: the denominator is a real audience's complete set of Facebook page likes (806 users; the 0.16% diet-share divides fake-news pages by TOTAL pages liked), which is the quantity the prevalence claim implies. Caveat recorded: only pages liked by >=2 respondents (25,080 of 141,693 distinct pages) were coded, so the numerator undercounts single-user fake-news likes - conservative, disclosed, does not overturn the LOW. Item 6 LOW: Grinberg et al. fact-checker-derived source list. Items 2-4 HIGH: MTurk convenience sample requiring app installation and consent, no response/attrition rate, explicitly non-representative of US Facebook users. Item 9 HIGH: page likes are an undated cumulative stock; the 5-day collection window (29 Dec 2016 - 2 Jan 2017) defines when, not over what period, exposure accrued.

quote_item6: News websites were those that adhere to journalistic norms, while our “junk” content was broken down into conspiracy (patently untrue or historically conspiratorial narratives); propaganda (websites that misrepresent facts for political ends); and sensationalism (factual websites that nevertheless emphasize salacious or “clickbait” perspectives).
quote_item10: In order to create similarly sized sample sets, we only coded websites with more than 2,000 mentions on Reddit and 400 on 4chan. This yielded 203 results from Reddit and 182 from 4chan.
notes: Item 6 HIGH: 'junk' explicitly bundles falsity (conspiracy) with tone and intent (sensationalism is defined as FACTUAL websites with clickbait framing), i.e. quality standing in for falsity - the archetypal CONTENT-vs-QUALITY failure. Item 7 HIGH: hostnames coded by 'qualitative observation of the front page', no reliability statistic, no validated list. Item 10 HIGH and the most severe in the shard: the 33.0%/20.0% are shares of UNIQUE HOSTNAMES that cleared arbitrary, platform-specific mention thresholds (>400 on 4chan, >2,000 on Reddit), not shares of links, posts or user exposure - so a hostname mentioned 401 times and one mentioned 4 million times count equally, and the two platform figures are not on a common denominator. Item 9 LOW: window stated (11 Jan 2019 - 25 Mar 2020).

quote_item6: We asked the annotators to select from four options: 1. Obviously not misinformation 2. Obvious misinformation 3. Already fact checked to be false 4. Needs concrete fact checking.

notes: Methodologically the strongest content analysis in the shard. Item 6 LOW: three professional fact-checking journalists with reverse-image-search against published fact-checks. Item 7 LOW: Fleiss kappa reported (0.78 two-class, 0.42 three-class). Item 3 LOW: 500 random + 2,000 most-shared images, with inverse-probability weighting and post-stratification back to the population of image shares - an explicit, correct fix for the popularity oversample. Item 10 still HIGH: the weighted denominator is image shares inside >5,000 keyword-found PUBLIC POLITICAL WhatsApp groups (images only, ~35% of content; text and video excluded), and the authors themselves state the prevalence figure 'may not generalize to the broader WhatsApp population'. Items 1-2 HIGH: groups found by manual keyword search of advertised invite links, with acknowledged heavy skew (24.4% BJP-affiliated vs 5% Congress).
